title: Thirty Guaraní towns on two rivers, run by one chain of command, 1609 to 1767
register: documentary, weighing the utopia and the slander against the ledger
summary: Guaraní communities and a handful of Jesuit priests built thirty towns across the Paraná and Uruguay watersheds, each at once a parish, a municipality with its own cabildo, a militia unit, and a way-station for yerba, hides, cattle, correspondence, and eventually muskets. Rivers carried the freight, a chain of command ran letters from a mission priest through the Superior at Candelaria to the provincial at Córdoba and on to Rome, and a Guaraní militia that first proved itself at Mbororé in 1641 became a standing reserve for the Crown it would later defy. Charles III's decree of 1767 ended Jesuit administration within a year or two; the towns, herds, cabildos, and river routes it left behind did not end with it.

nodes.name: San Ignacio Guazú
nodes.note: The conventional founding town of the whole system, traditionally dated to December 1609, though a rival reconstruction puts the first organized foundation in Guairá the same month. Early Paraná anchor for agriculture, workshops, and regional communication; its mission art survives in a local museum.

nodes.name: Nuestra Señora de la Encarnación de Itapúa
nodes.note: The principal Paraná crossing point between the Paraguay-side and Argentina-side towns, and the direct predecessor of the modern city.

nodes.name: Santiago de Caaguazú
nodes.note: Founded after earlier transfers, some of the population traceable to refugees from the broken Itatín missions. Agricultural and livestock node; the town survives under the same name.

nodes.name: Santa María de Fe
nodes.note: Sources disagree on whether 1647 or 1669 marks the predecessor or the final resettlement; some of its population came from the dissolved Itatín branch. Sculpture and church-related collections survive.

nodes.name: Santa Rosa de Lima
nodes.note: A daughter settlement of Santa María de Fe. A chapel belfry and mission art survive.

nodes.name: San Cosme y Damián
nodes.note: Moved after its initial founding. A river node whose workshops housed the astronomical and instrument-making work of Buenaventura Suárez; the church complex survives.

nodes.name: Jesús de Tavarangue
nodes.note: Its monumental church program was unfinished at the expulsion, leaving one of the clearest surviving records of how a reduction church was actually built. Now a UNESCO component site.

nodes.name: La Santísima Trinidad del Paraná
nodes.note: The last of the thirty mature towns to be founded, with an extensive stone complex and workshops. Now a UNESCO component site.

nodes.name: Corpus Christi
nodes.note: Transferred from the broken Guairá missions rather than founded outright. Paraná-side agricultural and river node; archaeological remains survive.

nodes.name: Nuestra Señora de Loreto
nodes.note: Founded in Guairá in 1610 and re-established here in 1631–32 after Ruiz de Montoya led the survivors of the Paulista destruction south. Became a major refugee town, a pilgrimage node, and the first home of the mission printing press.

nodes.name: San Ignacio Miní
nodes.note: Founded in Guairá in 1610 and moved here with Loreto during the 1631–32 exodus. Closely paired with Loreto; the monumental ruins and dense urban archaeology are among the best preserved of the thirty towns.

nodes.name: Santa Ana
nodes.note: Paraná-side production center; a UNESCO component site.

nodes.name: Nuestra Señora de Candelaria
nodes.note: For substantial periods the seat of the Superior of the Guaraní missions, and so the point where local correspondence entered the chain running to Córdoba and Rome. Also a major river crossing.

nodes.name: San José de Itacuá
nodes.note: An interior connector between the Paraná- and Uruguay-side towns.

nodes.name: Santos Apóstoles Pedro y Pablo
nodes.note: Agricultural and militia node; damaged in later warfare and less securely relocated on modern maps than most of the thirty.

nodes.name: Nuestra Señora de la Concepción de Ibitiracuá
nodes.modern: Concepción de la Sierra, Misiones, Argentina
nodes.note: One of the earliest Uruguay-side settlements and a major militia contributor, founded by Roque González's mission front.

nodes.name: Santos Mártires del Japón
nodes.modern: near Concepción de la Sierra, Misiones, Argentina
nodes.note: An offshoot and resettlement node whose ruins survive but whose precise modern footprint is less certain than the larger towns.

nodes.name: San Francisco Javier
nodes.note: A workshop node on the Uruguay River that later hosted the mission printing press.

nodes.name: Santa María la Mayor
nodes.note: Sources differ on whether 1626 or 1633 marks the predecessor or final transfer. Housed the printing press for a period. A UNESCO component site.

nodes.name: San Carlos Borromeo
nodes.note: A route and livestock node on the approaches to Corrientes.

nodes.name: Santo Tomé Apóstol
nodes.note: A Uruguay River crossing and communications hub; the modern town preserves the name and site.

nodes.name: Nuestra Señora de la Asunción de La Cruz
nodes.note: A riverine and military node associated with the Mbororé mobilization of 1641.

nodes.name: Nuestra Señora de los Reyes de Yapeyú
nodes.note: The southern terminus of the mission chain and the largest cattle-estate and transport hub in the network, with dependent territory reaching deep into the Banda Oriental.

nodes.name: São Francisco de Borja
nodes.modern: São Borja, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
nodes.note: First of the second-cycle eastern towns, founded after the eastern Tapé missions of the 1620s–30s had been destroyed. River and ranching center.

nodes.name: São Nicolau
nodes.modern: São Nicolau ruins, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
nodes.note: An earlier Tapé-era foundation re-established in 1687; a northeastern agricultural and strategic node, now an archaeological site.

nodes.name: São Luiz Gonzaga
nodes.modern: São Luiz Gonzaga, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
nodes.note: An interior production center of the Seven Peoples, near the site where the mission resistance was finally broken at Caiboaté in 1756. Modern town survives on the site.

nodes.name: São Miguel Arcanjo
nodes.modern: São Miguel das Missões, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
nodes.note: The largest monumental center of the eastern towns and the post of Sepé Tiarajú at the time of his death in 1756. UNESCO ruins and museum collections survive.

nodes.name: São Lourenço Mártir
nodes.modern: São Lourenço das Missões ruins, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
nodes.note: Ranching and agricultural node among the Seven Peoples; an archaeological site with less-precise modern siting than the larger towns.

nodes.name: São João Batista
nodes.modern: São João Batista ruins, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
nodes.note: Workshops and metallurgical and monumental production; an archaeological site.

nodes.name: Santo Ângelo Custódio
nodes.modern: Santo Ângelo, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
nodes.note: Last of the Seven Peoples, and its northern and eastern connector; the modern city preserves the name.

nodes.name: Guairá
nodes.region: then contested frontier, now Paraná state, Brazil
nodes.note: About thirteen missions established between roughly 1610 and 1628 in the region bounded by the Paraná, Paranapanema, Tibagi, and Piquiri rivers. Jesuit reports claimed more than 40,000 residents, an institutional figure rather than an independent census. Paulista slaving expeditions destroyed most of the settlements by 1631; survivors made the roughly 500-kilometer exodus south that refounded Loreto and San Ignacio Miní. Placed here at the modern town of Guaíra, which preserves the region's name, not at a single mission site.

nodes.name: Itatín
nodes.region: then frontier north/east of Asunción, now Paraguay and Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil
nodes.note: A mission branch north and east of Asunción broken by Paulista attacks, Mbayá pressure, epidemics, and relocation. Some refugee populations fed the later towns of Santiago and Santa María de Fe, though continuity between successive names is often hard to demonstrate. The dossier gives no firm founding date; placed here only approximately.

nodes.name: Asunción
nodes.note: The older Spanish town the reductions grew up beside, and the diocesan seat whose bishop retained sacramental and visitation authority over the missions even as the Jesuits ran their day-to-day government. A procurator and commercial relay point for exports moving toward Santa Fe and Buenos Aires.

nodes.name: Santa Fe
nodes.region: Governorate of Río de la Plata
nodes.note: A Jesuit procurator seat downstream on the Paraná where mission yerba, hides, and cotton were sold or bartered for cloth, iron, and wine, and where documented obligations such as the 1659 exchange of yerba for cloth were settled.

nodes.name: Buenos Aires
nodes.region: Governorate of Río de la Plata
nodes.note: The other principal procurator seat and the port through which Atlantic goods entered and the missions' exports could in principle reach Europe. Also the port through which the arrested Jesuits were shipped toward exile after 1767.

nodes.name: Córdoba
nodes.note: Administrative seat of the Jesuit Province of Paraguay, which was far larger than the thirty Guaraní towns and also encompassed colleges, farms, and other missions. Correspondence from the Superior at Candelaria passed through here on its way to consultors and eventually to Rome.

nodes.name: Rome
nodes.note: Seat of the Jesuit superior general, the formal endpoint of the Cartas Anuas correspondence chain that ran from mission priest through Candelaria and Córdoba. No evidence in the dossier fixes an exact date the chain first reached Rome from Paraguay; it is bounded here to the network's own period.

nodes.name: The Society of Jesus, Province of Paraguay
nodes.note: Authorized as an independent province in 1604, this was the corporate body that gave the thirty towns a common rule, a common correspondence chain, and common personnel, even though most towns held only two or three Jesuits at a time. Dissolved in its temporal authority over the missions by Charles III's Pragmatic Sanction of 2 April 1767.

nodes.name: Diego de Torres Bollo
nodes.note: First provincial of the newly independent Jesuit Province of Paraguay, and the organizer whose mission program produced San Ignacio Guazú and the first Guairá foundations. His years here mark his service organizing the province, not his full biography; he later moved on to other Jesuit provincial duties.

nodes.name: Roque González de Santa Cruz
nodes.note: A Paraguayan-born Jesuit who founded or organized Itapúa, Concepción, Yapeyú, and other southern missions. Killed on 15 November 1628 at Caaró during Indigenous resistance to the mission program, an opposition that Jesuit martyrological sources frame through a theological lens.

nodes.name: Antonio Ruiz de Montoya
nodes.note: Superior, chronicler, and organizer of the Guairá evacuation of 1631–32, later a petitioner in the imperial system for firearms and against Indigenous enslavement; his lobbying helped produce the royal order of 21 May 1640 that regularized the arming of mission militia. His dates here mark active service to the network's defense and legal standing, not his full life.

nodes.name: Buenaventura Suárez
nodes.note: A Jesuit specialist in astronomy and instrument-making based at San Cosme y Damián. The dossier does not give exact tenure dates; the range here is approximate, drawn from the general chronology of the mission's scientific activity rather than a documented appointment and death date.

nodes.name: Sepé Tiarajú
nodes.note: An official of São Miguel who became the leading Guaraní commander resisting the forced relocation ordered under the 1750 Treaty of Madrid. Killed 7 February 1756, days before the resistance was crushed at Caiboaté. The phrase associated with him, 'this land has owners,' belongs to political memory rather than a securely attested verbatim quotation.

nodes.name: Nicolás Ñeengirú
nodes.note: The name Nicolás Ñeengirú appears twice in the record 115 years apart: as the Guaraní commander at Mbororé in March 1641, and as 'Ñeengirú/Nanguirú,' an Indigenous commander killed at Caiboaté in 1756. Treated here as one entry for the recurring title, but the gap makes it far more likely these are two different men sharing a name or office than one man active across more than a century; the dossier does not resolve this, and the same name was later attached, without evidence, to the propagandistic legend of a Jesuit-controlled 'Nicolás I, King of Paraguay.'

nodes.name: The Guaraní militia
nodes.note: Armed and organized under Indigenous commanders from the late 1630s, formally regularized by the royal order of 21 May 1640, and proven at Mbororé in 1641. A 1647 inventory recorded 609 firearms distributed among missions, with 150 more supplied under a 1649 decree. The same force that defended towns against Paulista slavers became a standing frontier reserve for the Crown, and, a century later, the core of the resistance the Crown and Portugal crushed at Caiboaté in 1756.

nodes.name: The Spanish Crown
nodes.note: Royal patronage authorized the reduction policy, governors and audiencias regulated tribute and labor, and the same Crown that licensed the mission militia in 1640 dissolved Jesuit authority over the towns by Charles III's Pragmatic Sanction of 2 April 1767, implemented in the Río de la Plata the following year under governor Francisco de Paula Bucareli y Ursúa.

nodes.name: The yerba trade
nodes.note: The network's principal export and its main source of imported cloth, iron, and wine. A 1659 obligation exchanged 79 arrobas of yerba for cloth; a 1675 obligation exchanged 217 arrobas and 18 pounds for luxury textiles, gold lace, silk stockings, and leather. A 1683-era complaint from the Jesuit superior general also accused procurators of reselling yerba and other goods for markups they could not adequately account for.

nodes.name: The mission printing press
nodes.note: Began operating about 1700, first at Loreto, then moved among Santa María la Mayor and San Francisco Javier. Produced Guaraní-language and bilingual religious works, including Nicolás Yapuguay's 'Sermones y ejemplos' of 1727. The equipment was locally fashioned to a considerable degree, though claims that every component was mission-made are hard to verify.

nodes.name: The Cartas Anuas correspondence chain
nodes.note: The regular chain of narrative reports running from mission priest or cabildo through the Superior of Missions at Candelaria, the provincial at Córdoba, and consultors, to the Jesuit general in Rome. Surviving collections record foundations, conversions, conflicts, epidemics, and finances, but are selective institutional documents written for governance and edification rather than a neutral ledger.
